text:
**The Chair on Delancey Lane**

The city had been warned, but the city had been warned before, and so on the afternoon the river began to come up through the storm drains, people were still out buying bread. I was one of them, though I had no intention of buying bread. I had nothing in particular to do that day. That is perhaps the most important thing to say about me, and the least interesting.

I saw them outside the pharmacy on Merritt Street. A man and a woman, perhaps in their late forties. He wore a yellow windbreaker. She wore a gray wool coat, an unwise choice for the weather, and carried a paper bag that had begun to darken at the bottom. There was nothing remarkable about them. Their faces seemed assembled from spare parts of other faces.

And yet I stopped, my hand on the pharmacy door, and watched them walk away, and felt something like a word on the tip of my tongue. As if they were a name I had once known.

I followed them. It did not feel like a decision.

He held an umbrella, mostly over her. She did not seem to notice the rain, or the umbrella, or him. At the corner of Merritt and Delancey Lane, they stopped in front of a chair.

It was an armchair, or had been. Someone had set it on the curb beside a pile of trash bags, and at some point it had been set on fire. A strip of the original fabric survived along the bottom, the green of a pool table. The rest had gone a crackled black, like the skin on a pudding. One arm had burned through to the frame, and the springs of the seat stood up in a little coiled crowd. There was still a smell, sweet and chemical, that reached me in the doorway of a closed dry cleaner.

The man said something and laughed. The woman did not laugh. She reached out and laid her palm flat against the back of the chair, the way you might lay your hand on the flank of a horse. She kept it there. The man stopped laughing. He looked at the chair, then at her, then up and down the street, the way people look when they suddenly feel they are not alone with their own lives.

After a while, he touched her elbow, and she took her hand away, and they went on.

I paused beside the chair. I did not touch it. I only looked at the place where her hand had been. The char there was smoother, as though her palm had polished it.

They lived four blocks on, in the ground-floor apartment of a narrow brick building whose front steps had already disappeared. The water in the street was at my ankles, brown and quick and full of small things: bottle caps, a child's sock. They went in through a side door, and a lamp came on in the front window.

I stood beneath a linden tree across the street and watched.

So little happened. The man hung his windbreaker on a hook and came back with two plates. The woman sat in a wooden chair near the window. She did not take off her coat. He set a plate before her and began to eat, and she did not eat, and he did not seem to expect her to.

The water rose to my shins. I thought, quite calmly, that I should go home. I thought that I had no particular reason to.

As the light outside failed and the window grew brighter, like a painting being finished, I noticed the way she sat: very upright, her arms along the arms of the chair, her hands curled over the ends. Her coat, soaked through, looked darker now, and it fell over the seat so that it was hard to tell where the coat ended and the chair began. Her hair had dried in stiff black tufts. Now and then the man spoke, and she turned her head toward him, very slightly, and then back toward the window, toward me, though I do not think she could see me.

The water reached my knees. It was cold in a way that seemed to have opinions.

At around eight, the power went out, block by block, like someone walking through a house closing doors. When it reached their building, the lamp went out. Then the man lit a candle and set it between them.

By candlelight, she was only a shape. I could see the outline of her shoulders, the line of one arm, the place where her hands should have been, and above all that a dense blackness, crackled where the light caught it, as if she had been heated and cooled too fast. The man leaned toward her and laid his palm flat against her shoulder, and he kept it there.

Something nudged the back of my legs.

I turned slowly, because the water was heavy and because I already knew. The chair had come down Delancey Lane on the current. It bumped against me again, gently, like a dog that wants to be let in. The springs stood up out of the brown water, beaded with rain.

When I looked back, the candle had gone out. There was only the glass, and in it a faint reflection: the tree, the water, and a figure standing waist-deep beside a ruined chair, both very still, both facing the house, as though waiting to be asked inside.

The rescue boats came through sometime after midnight. A young woman in an orange vest pulled me in, wrapped me in a foil blanket, and asked if anyone else was in the area. I said I didn't know, which was true. I pointed at the window. They shone the light in. The room was empty: a small table, two plates, a hook with nothing on it.

No chair. I looked for the other one in the water, but it was gone too.

I have walked past the building many times since. The apartment has been gutted and repainted and is for rent. I have not called the number. On Merritt and Delancey there is a new pile of trash bags every Thursday, and I find that I slow down when I pass it, and that I put out my hand, and that I am not sure, anymore, what I am hoping to touch.
